summary: Lets a SIP user agent that receives a dialog-forming request tell the peer its identity, in a request in the reverse direction, with the identity signed by an Authentication Service. This matters because retargeting can change who actually answers. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When you call and a different person answers, you want to know who really picked up. This lets the answerer tell you their name in a way that can be checked.

questions: what is connected identity in sip
how does sip report who answered a call
what is the from-change option tag
how does sip update identity during a call
why does sip use update for identity
subtitle: How a SIP phone can tell its peer who really answered, with a signature that can be checked.

tldr.problem: When a SIP call is retargeted, for example by call forwarding, the person who answers can differ from the person named in the To header field. The same happens when a party is replaced mid-call, for instance by a transfer.
tldr.mechanism: The party whose identity changed sends a request in the reverse direction, normally UPDATE, with its identity in the From header field URI. An Authentication Service on the path can sign that identity using the Identity header field from RFC 4474.
tldr.outcome: Callers can learn, and verify, who is really connected. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261 by no longer requiring the original To and From URIs to be repeated in later mid-dialog requests.

today: RFC 4916 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3261 and relies on the Identity mechanism of RFC 4474.

sections.title: Who Is Really Connected
sections.content:
SIP shows the parties at both ends of a call, but the person who answers can differ from the one first called. Call forwarding, call distribution and call pick-up can cause this. Later, a party can be replaced by call transfer, call park and retrieval, and similar actions.

RFC 4916 extends the use of the From header field to carry what is commonly called connected identity, the identity of the connected user, in either direction inside an existing INVITE-initiated dialog. It can convey the callee identity when a call is answered, the identity of a potential callee before answer, or the identity of a user who replaces the caller or callee after a rearrangement done in the PSTN or in a B2BUA.

Identity in a response (response identity) is outside the scope. The RFC notes it would be hard to authenticate the UAS that way, while a separate request lets normal authentication techniques be used. Ordinary REFER-based transfer creates a new dialog, so the normal caller and callee identity mechanisms already apply.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the person who picks up is not the one you dialed, or a call gets handed to someone else. This document gives a way to say who is on the line now.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. The caller is the user of the UA that sends the INVITE. The callee is the user of the UA that answers by sending a 2xx response. A potential callee is the user of any UA the INVITE reaches and forms an early dialog with, though forking means that user may not be the one who answers.

A connected user is anyone involved in an established call, including a user who replaces the caller or callee after a re-arrangement such as transfer. A connected identity is that user's Address of Record.
sections.eli5: The caller starts the call, the callee answers it, and a connected user is anyone who is on the call right now, even if they took over from someone else.

sections.title: How the Solution Works
sections.content:
A mid-dialog request carries the connected identity. The UA that sends it puts its identity in the From header field URI. An Authentication Service on the path adds the Identity header field from RFC 4474. Unless it sits at the UAC, that service is expected to be at a proxy that record routes and can authenticate the UAC.

The method is UPDATE (RFC 3311), or in some cases re-INVITE. The callee sends UPDATE after its 2xx response and after receiving an ACK. For a potential callee, it sends UPDATE after receiving and answering a PRACK, which follows a reliable 1xx response (RFC 3262). A re-INVITE is used for a mid-call change when it is needed anyway, for example when a B2BUA doing third party call control has to send a re-INVITE without an SDP offer.

This changes the URI, not the tags, in the To and From header fields of mid-dialog requests and responses. RFC 3261 had expected mandatory reflection of the original URIs to be deprecated later, and this document does so. A new option tag, from-change, in the Supported header field signals that a UA tolerates the change, so it never needs to go in a Require header field.

A UA that received a connected identity in a From URI must use that URI in the To header field of its later mid-dialog requests. Without an Authentication Service on the path, the identity arrives unauthenticated.
sections.eli5: The person who answers sends a small follow-up message saying who they are, and a trusted helper along the way can stamp it so it is believable.

sections.title: What Each Party Must Do
sections.content:
A UA that sends an INVITE MUST include from-change in the Supported header field. A UA that receives an INVITE MUST include it in any dialog-forming response. Sending the tag does not guarantee that a connected identity will arrive.

Once an early dialog exists and the peer has sent from-change, the receiving UA MAY send an UPDATE, provided it sent a reliable provisional response and has received and answered a PRACK. After sending a 2xx, it MUST send an UPDATE if it has not already done so. The UPDATE carries the callee's or potential callee's identity in the From URI, or an anonymous identity if anonymity is required. Even when the URI matches the INVITE's To URI, the new request lets the Authentication Service vouch for it.

If a UA's identity changes during a dialog, for example by transfer, and the peer advertised from-change, it MUST send a request with the new identity, using UPDATE unless a re-INVITE is already being sent.

Sending a mid-dialog request, a UA follows RFC 4474 when filling in the From URI and puts the current remote URI in To. After revising its From URI it keeps sending the same one unless the identity changes again. It must accept the revised URI in To, and the old one until a request with the revised URI has been received. On receiving a request with a different From URI, the UA MUST update the remote URI only if it sends a 2xx response, and MUST NOT after any other final response.

If the UAC gets a 428, 436, 437 or 438 response, it SHOULD treat the dialog as terminated for a dialog-terminating request, and take no action for other requests. A UA receiving a signed identity SHOULD invoke a Verifier if it cannot rely on one on the path.
sections.eli5: Both phones say they can handle name changes. After someone answers, they send a name tag message, and from then on both sides use the new name.

sections.title: Authentication Services and Proxies
sections.content:
An Authentication Service MUST follow RFC 4474 for mid-dialog requests. That RFC is silent on what to do if the From identity is not one the UAC may assert, so it is local policy whether to reject the request or forward it with no Identity header field. The policy may differ for mid-dialog requests.

Because UAs that follow this document send their real identity in From, the Authentication Service can authenticate the sender as the entity in From and sign it. For UAs that do not follow it, retargeting and mid-dialog changes can make From an inaccurate guide to the sender.

A Verifier follows RFC 4474 too. RFC 4474 leaves it to policy whether to reject a request lacking an Identity header field with a 428 response, and a UA MAY use a different policy for mid-dialog requests.

A proxy MUST be ready for the To and From URIs to differ from those in the dialog-forming request and response. A proxy that can provide an Authentication Service MUST record route if the dialog-forming request it received from the UAC indicated Supported: from-change.
sections.eli5: A trusted helper in the middle can sign the name tag. It has to stay on the path of the call, and it must not be confused when names change.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example has Alice call Bob. The proxy retargets the call to Carol's UA, which answers. Carol's UA then sends an UPDATE with From: Carol and the same tag as in the INVITE response. The proxy acts as the Authentication Service and adds Identity and Identity-Info header fields before it reaches Alice.

The second example has a call between Alice and Bob, who sits behind a B2BUA. Bob's identity is sent by UPDATE. The B2BUA then transfers the call with third party call control, so Alice becomes connected to Carol, and it sends a re-INVITE with Carol in From plus an Identity header field. Both examples use from-change, and the second shows an ACK carrying Carol's session description.
sections.eli5: In one story the call is passed on and the new person introduces themselves. In the other a call is handed from Bob to Carol and Alice is told.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4474 discusses the Identity header field's security considerations in detail, and they apply here. A From URI in a mid-dialog request with no valid Identity header field, or other authentication, cannot be trusted except in very closed environments. It is expected to be treated like an unsigned From in a dialog-initiating request.

The RFC recommends not rejecting a mid-dialog request just because Identity is missing, since that would disturb the call. The missing signature can shape what the user is told, and a UA may clear the call if policy or the user requires.

A signed identity says nothing about whether retargeting or an identity change was legitimate; it only reflects the result. History information (RFC 4244) can add hints about how the user was reached. Using a sips URI can reduce the chance of attacks sending inappropriate connected identity. Anonymity is handled as RFC 4474 describes.
sections.eli5: A name with a signature can be trusted more than one without. The signature shows who it is, not whether it was fair that they took the call.

sections.title: The from-change Option Tag
sections.content: The only IANA action is a new SIP option tag, from-change, added to the Option Tags registry of the SIP Parameter Registry. Its description is that it indicates a UA supports changes to URIs in From and To header fields during a dialog.
sections.eli5: The new label that a phone uses to say it can handle name changes is written in the official list of labels.

items.title: From URI
items.text: Holds the identity of the sender of the mid-dialog request.

items.title: UPDATE or re-INVITE
items.text: The request used to carry the new From URI.

items.title: Identity header
items.text: Added by an Authentication Service to sign the identity (RFC 4474).

items.title: from-change
items.text: Option tag in Supported that says the UA tolerates URI changes.
